An error, because the value is out of range
0, because unknown values default to zero
About 4.2, outside the range the model was trained on
explain: Min-max uses the stored constants: (400000 - 12) / (95000 - 12) is about 4.2. A linear model extrapolates past anything it saw; a tree treats it like the largest training value. Clipping, log transforms or rank-based encodings make this less surprising.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: You switch your nDCG@10 code from log2 to natural log in the discount, keeping everything else fixed. What happens to the scores?
options: Every nDCG@10 changes by the factor ln 2
Nothing: the constant factor cancels between DCG and ideal DCG
Ranks 1 and 2 become undiscounted
nDCG can now exceed 1
explain: log_e(i+1) = ln 2 times log2(i+1) for every rank, so both the run's DCG and the ideal DCG are scaled by the same factor 1/ln 2, which cancels. Raw DCG does change, and so does the original Jarvelin-Kekalainen form, where the base also decides how many ranks escape discounting.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
question: You already use `sendfile` so the server never copies file bytes into user space. Which cost does RDMA remove that `sendfile` still pays?
options: Running the transport protocol and a system call on the host CPU for each message
The copy from the page cache into a socket buffer
The DMA from host memory to the NIC
The need to know the destination address
explain: `sendfile` already avoids the user-space copy, and DMA between memory and the NIC happens in both designs. What stays with sockets is the kernel: a system call per operation and the TCP stack running on a CPU per packet. RDMA moves the transport into the NIC and lets the application post work without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
question: You want one server to accept requests from 10,000 clients with as little NIC state as possible. Which transport fits, and what does it give up?
options: UD: one QP can talk to every client, but only SEND/RECV of at most one MTU per message
RC: it supports every verb
UC: it is unreliable, so it needs no state
UD: it supports RDMA READ without connections
explain: A connected QP (RC or UC) talks to exactly one peer, so 10,000 clients need 10,000 QPs. A UD QP can exchange datagrams with any UD QP, which is why designs like HERD use it for responses. The price: no RDMA READ/WRITE or atomics, no reliability, and single-MTU messages.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
question: A server receives a client frame whose MASK bit is 0. What does RFC 6455 require?
options: Close the connection, optionally with close code 1002 (protocol error)
Unmask it with a zero key and process it normally
Reply with a ping to ask the client to resend it masked
Accept it only if the connection is over TLS
explain: Section 5.1: the server MUST close the connection on an unmasked client frame and MAY send close code 1002. Masking is required whether or not TLS is used, so TLS does not make it optional.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: Your game streams 20 snapshots per second over WebSocket at 150 ms RTT on a lossy mobile link. Players see enemies freeze then jump. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Enable TCP_NODELAY on the server
Move snapshots to an unreliable channel such as WebTransport datagrams, keeping reliable messages on a stream
Lower the patch rate to 5 per second
Switch from t.float32() to t.number()
explain: The freeze-then-burst pattern is head-of-line blocking: a lost packet holds back later snapshots until retransmission. TCP_NODELAY only disables Nagle batching. An unreliable channel lets newer snapshots through, and the interpolation buffer skips the gap.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
question: A two-tower model trained with plain in-batch softmax rarely retrieves the top-100 hit items, even for users who like them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hit items appear in many batches, so they are used as negatives far more often and get pushed down; apply the logQ correction
The temperature is too high, so all scores are equal
Hit items have too few training examples
Normalizing embeddings removes popularity information
explain: In-batch negatives follow the traffic distribution, which is power-law. Yi et al. note popular items are overly penalized as negatives and subtract log p_j from each logit to correct the bias.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters
question: A colleague fits H from the card corners, but lists the mm points in the order TL, BL, BR, TR while the pixel points are TL, TR, BR, BL. What happens?
options: H maps the card onto a transposed card, so lengths along the card's width and height are swapped and measurements are wrong
OpenCV automatically sorts the points, so nothing changes
The fit fails with an error because the points are not in clockwise order
Only the sign of the result flips
explain: The solver trusts the pairing you give it. Swapped pairs still define a valid homography, just to a wrong rectangle (85.6 placed along the 53.98 side), so it returns confidently wrong numbers. This is why ArUco returns corners in a fixed order.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
question: For parallel aggregation, two workers compute partial results for group a. Worker 1 saw 30; worker 2 saw 50 and 40. What should the final step combine to get avg = 40?
options: The two averages, 30 and 45, averaged to 37.5
The two states (1, 30) and (2, 90), added to (3, 120), then 120 / 3
Only the larger worker's average, 45
The two averages weighted equally, then rounded
explain: Averaging averages gives 37.5, which is wrong. The correct merge combines transition states: counts add and sums add, then the final function divides once. PostgreSQL supports this with combine functions for partial aggregation; the merge works on states, not on finished results.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Latency: you wait for the slowest replica you need
question: N = 5, replica delays independent with the same distribution. Which choice gives the lowest 99.9th percentile write latency while still overlapping reads done with R = 3?
explain: Overlap needs R + W > 5, so with R = 3 the smallest valid W is 3. Latency only grows with W (you wait for a later order statistic), so W = 3 is the fastest correct choice. W = 1 or 2 is faster but breaks the overlap.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
question: Same house, true reward [1, 1, 1]. A new proxy over-weights the attic: [3, 1, 1]. Using the 8 deterministic policies, is it hackable?
options: No: it gives positive weight to every room, so it agrees with the true reward
Yes: A alone gets proxy 3 but true 1, while B+K gets proxy 2 but true 2
No: over-weighting one room only changes ties, never strict orderings
Yes, but only for stochastic policies
explain: The proxy prefers A (3 over 2) while the true reward prefers B+K (2 over 1): a strict reversal. Positive weights on every room are not enough. A milder proxy [2, 1, 1] would tie A with B+K (2 and 2) and, by exhaustive check, has no strict reversal.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
question: A team switches its GRPO run from a 4k to a 32k maximum response length. Training time per token is unchanged. Which stage's share of the step most likely grows?
options: Rollout, because decode steps are sequential and the batch waits for its longest response
The optimizer step, because more tokens produce larger gradients
Reference logprobs, because the reference model is frozen
Weight sync, because longer responses need more weight bytes
explain: Rollout grows most: each extra token is one more sequential decode step, and a synchronous batch waits for its longest member. The optimizer step and weight sync do not depend on response length, and the logprob passes are parallel over tokens.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: NeMo RL async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. A trajectory was generated with weights v10. At which training steps can it be used?
options: Steps 10 and 11; at step 12 it is discarded
Only step 10
Steps 9, 10 and 11
Any step, as long as importance sampling correction is on
explain: The docs' own example: a trajectory generated with v10 can be used for training steps v10 or v11, and at step v12 it is too old and is discarded. Importance correction handles the remaining mismatch; it does not remove the age limit.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
question: Your Alertmanager groups by alert name only, not by service. During this incident the group named ServiceLatencyHigh contains alerts from checkout, pricing, catalog and cart. What have you lost?
options: Nothing: grouping is lossless, and the labels are still in the notification
The error-ratio alerts, because grouping keeps only one alert type per group
The ability to see at a glance which services are affected and which are not, because one group now hides the per-service pattern that points at the cause
The SLO burn alert, which is always inhibited by instance-level alerts
explain: Grouping is lossless in principle (the labels travel with the group), but the grouping key decides what the notification shows you first. Grouping by name alone merges unrelated services into one blob and destroys exactly the signal you want: which parts of the graph are anomalous. Group by something that preserves topology, such as alert name plus service or cluster.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
question: At 20:22 you are 90 percent sure catalog's pool config is the cause but you do not know how the value 4 got rendered. What do you do?
options: Keep digging until you understand the rendering, so the revert cannot make things worse
Revert the config now, confirm the symptom clears, and work out how the value got rendered afterwards
Raise the pool to 128 to add margin, since you are unsure of the right value
Wait for the config owner to wake up, since they can explain the render
explain: Reverting to a state the system ran in minutes ago is the lowest-risk action available, and the recovery is itself evidence for your hypothesis. Understanding the template can happen with users served. Raising the pool to 128 sounds prudent but changes to an untested value, and waiting for the config owner extends a user-visible outage for a conversation.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
question: Why does a single off-topic rewrite in RAG-Fusion usually do limited damage to the fused list?
options: RRF detects off-topic queries and drops them
RRF uses the cosine scores, which are lower for off-topic results
Its documents get at most one vote of about 1/61, while documents shared by several rewrites collect several votes
The LLM answer step re-sorts documents by relevance
explain: RRF knows nothing about topicality. The protection is structural: a document returned by only one of four lists can reach about 1/61, while documents several lists agree on get two to four votes. The same mechanism also buries a uniquely good rewrite's finds.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Pinning: building kernel objects where they will live
question: A developer writes `fn new() -> Mutex<u32>` that builds the mutex on the stack and returns it. Why does the kernel API not offer this?
options: Returning moves the value, so `__mutex_init` would have run at the old address and the C object would move afterwards
Kernel stacks are too small to hold a mutex
Mutexes can only be global statics in the kernel
Rust functions cannot return generic types in no_std
explain: Return by value is a move. The C mutex would be initialized at one address and used at another, breaking self pointers such as the debug `magic` field. `Mutex::new` therefore returns `impl PinInit<Self>`, and the caller chooses where it lives before it is initialized.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
question: Your scheduler's select_cpu always returns CPU 0 for every task but never inserts anything. Your enqueue puts every task in one shared custom DSQ, and dispatch moves from it. Where do tasks actually run?
options: On whichever CPU calls dispatch and moves them to its local DSQ, so across all CPUs
Only on CPU 0, because select_cpu pins the task there
On CPU 0 for the first slice, then anywhere
The core rejects the scheduler for returning the same CPU every time
explain: select_cpu's return value is a non-binding hint (and the CPU it wakes if idle). Without an insertion there, the task goes through enqueue into the shared DSQ, and any CPU running dispatch can move it to its own local DSQ.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 3, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: In `tip_suggestion`, what happens when Python executes `f += sgl.gen(...)` for fork 0?
options: Python blocks until fork 0's paragraph is fully generated, then moves to fork 1
Both forks are concatenated into a single request with one long prompt
The call is submitted to fork 0's stream and returns at once, so fork 1 is submitted right away and the runtime can batch them
The function is compiled into a CUDA graph before any request is sent
explain: The interpreter runs each prompt state as an asynchronous stream: `gen` is non-blocking, like a kernel launch. Only reading a result (`forks[0]["detailed_tip"]`) waits. That is what gives intra-program parallelism.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: An OSM way is tagged `oneway=yes` and runs from node u to node v. How does it appear in a directed road graph such as an OSMnx MultiDiGraph?
options: As two arcs, u to v and v to u, with the second marked as forbidden
As an undirected edge with a flag that routing code checks
As a single arc from u to v
It is dropped, because one-way streets cannot be routed
explain: Direction is encoded in the graph itself: a one-way street contributes only the arc u to v, while a two-way street contributes two reciprocal arcs. The search then simply never finds a way to travel v to u on that street.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: Your service ingests new traffic speeds every few minutes and must route with them right away. Which OSRM setup fits the docs' guidance?
options: MLD: partition once, rerun osrm-customize with the new speed file
CH, rerunning osrm-contract every few minutes
Plain Dijkstra with no preprocessing
CH with osrm-customize
explain: osrm-customize applies speed and turn-penalty files to a partitioned MLD graph and can be rerun without re-partitioning. CH's contraction would have to be redone, and osrm-customize is not part of the CH pipeline. Plain Dijkstra is far too slow at continental scale.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Convolution, the convolution theorem and FIR filters
question: You compute `ifft(fft(x) * fft(h, len(x)))` to convolve a 1000-sample signal with a 50-tap kernel, and the first 49 output samples look wrong. Why?
options: The FFT is only approximate for lengths that are not powers of two
The DFT product gives circular convolution, so the tail of the output wrapped around onto the start
The kernel must be reversed before the FFT
fft(h, len(x)) truncates the kernel
explain: Multiplying DFTs is circular convolution. The full linear result has 1000 + 50 - 1 = 1049 samples; with only 1000 bins the last 49 wrap onto the first 49. Zero-pad both to at least 1049 (scipy.signal.fftconvolve does this for you).

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Using the model with t_c = 0.54 ns, b = 12 bytes, BW = 30 GB/s, what is the best speedup any lane count can give?
options: About 4x
About 16x
About 1.35x
Unlimited
explain: The memory term is 12 / 30 = 0.4 ns per element and scalar compute is 0.54 ns. With infinite lanes time drops to 0.4 ns, so the speedup is at most 0.54 / 0.4 = 1.35x.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: In the last scene, 32 bytes are free yet a 32-byte request fails. Which term names this problem?
options: Internal fragmentation, because the blocks are too large for their contents
External fragmentation, because the free space is split into holes smaller than the request
A memory leak, because B and D were never returned to the allocator
Alignment padding, because 32-byte blocks must start on a 32-byte boundary
explain: B and D were freed correctly, so it is not a leak. The free bytes exist but are scattered into two 16-byte holes, which is external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation is waste *inside* a handed-out block.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A driver calls `kmalloc(260)` a million times. Roughly how much memory is lost to size-class rounding, and what is the usual fix?
options: About 0.25 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 512; give the type its own kmem_cache
Nothing, because kmalloc returns exactly the requested size
About 0.06 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 320; use vmalloc instead
About 0.5 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 1024; allocate whole pages with alloc_pages
explain: The classes go 256 then 512, so each 260-byte request occupies 512 bytes: 252 bytes x 1,000,000 = 252 MB, about 0.25 GB. A dedicated cache sized for the object (kmem_cache_create) removes almost all of that waste.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: Rollout takes 300 s, training 300 s and sync 48 s per round on separate pools. Ignoring all overheads, what is the best case for fully async?
options: 348 s per round, about 1.86x faster than 648 s
648 s per round, the same as sync
300 s per round
48 s per round
explain: The bound is max(t_R, t_T) + t_W = 300 + 48 = 348 s against 300 + 300 + 48 = 648 s serial. Weight sync is not hidden in this model, so the round cannot drop to 300 s.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: You switch an SAE from L1 to TopK and keep everything else the same. Which hyperparameter replaces lambda as the main sparsity knob?
options: k, the number of latents kept per token
The learning rate
The number of latents M
The kernel bandwidth epsilon
explain: TopK sets sparsity directly: L0 equals k. There is no sparsity term in the loss, so there is no lambda to tune. Epsilon belongs to JumpReLU training.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
question: You switch an IDW map from p = 1 to p = 6. What happens to the map?
options: It approaches nearest neighbor: flat patches around each sensor with sharper transitions between them
It becomes smoother everywhere
It starts extrapolating trends beyond the readings
Nothing, because weights are normalized
explain: A large power makes the nearest sensor dominate, so the map looks like Voronoi tiles with steeper transitions. Normalization keeps weights summing to 1, but it does not undo the change in their ratios.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Why can the target model score 5 guessed tokens in roughly the time it takes to generate 1 token at batch size 1?
options: The target skips attention for guessed tokens
Guessed tokens use a lower precision path
The GPU runs 5 separate copies of the model in parallel
At small batch the step is memory bound: weights and KV cache are read once either way, and 5 token vectors add little arithmetic
explain: The cost of a small-batch decode step is dominated by reading weights and KV cache from memory. Multiplying those weights by 5 vectors instead of 1 adds arithmetic the chip has to spare, so latency barely changes (Chen et al.'s argument for linear layers, attention and all-reduces).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: With s1 = 3, s2 = 2, s3 = 2, how many tree nodes must the target verify in one pass?
explain: Level sizes are 3, 3 x 2 = 6 and 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, for 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 nodes. Twelve full candidate paths share their prefixes, which is why tree attention is cheaper than 12 separate sequences of length 3.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
question: A CTC model must output the word too. Which frame path collapses to too?
options: t o o
t t o o o
t o _ o
_ t o o _
explain: Merging repeats turns t o o, t t o o o and _ t o o _ into to (or _to_, then to). Only t o _ o keeps two separate o runs, because the blank breaks the run before merging. Removing the blank then gives too.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: For virtual address 0x00007f3a12345678 mapped with a 2 MiB huge page, which bits form the offset within the page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 20 to 0
Bits 29 to 0
Bits 47 to 21
explain: A 2 MiB page is $2^{21}$ bytes, so the offset is the low 21 bits (here 0x145678). The PMD entry maps the page directly, so bits 20 to 12, which would normally index a PTE table, become part of the offset.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: You build a CAA vector from 300 pairs where every positive prompt happens to be longer than its negative partner. What is the most likely problem?
options: None: averaging over 300 pairs removes all confounds
The vector partly encodes prompt length, because that difference is consistent across pairs and does not average out
The vector will have length zero
Mean difference only works with exactly one pair
explain: Averaging cancels differences that vary randomly across pairs. A difference that is the same in every pair, such as length, survives averaging and becomes part of the vector. CAA avoids this by making each pair identical except for one answer letter.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
question: A gateway loses its uplink for 30 s and then forwards all buffered readings at once. You compute per-10 s averages by processing time. What happens to the 30 s of readings?
options: They are averaged into the windows in which they were measured, just later
They all land in the single window in which they arrived, and the three earlier windows show missing data
Kafka reorders them by event time before the processor sees them
MQTT QoS 1 guarantees they are delivered in event-time order
explain: Processing-time windows bucket by arrival. The burst lands in one window (inflating its count) and the earlier windows look empty. Kafka keeps the order in which records were written to a partition; it does not sort by event time.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Which design gives the most useful long-term history for detecting rare overheating at the lowest storage cost?
options: Keep raw readings forever
Keep raw data for days and 1-minute rollups with count, mean, min and max for years
Keep only 1-hour means for years
Keep only the latest reading per sensor
explain: Short raw retention covers debugging, and long-lived rollups with min and max keep the extremes that a mean hides, at a fraction of the rows. Hourly means alone would average away a 30 second overheat.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
question: You remove the positional encodings from a trained encoder and feed it "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". What happens to the encoder output for the token "man"?
options: It is identical in both sentences
It differs, because attention weights depend on which tokens are nearby
It differs, because the FFN processes positions in order
It becomes all zeros
explain: Without positional information, self-attention and the position-wise FFN are permutation equivariant. Both sentences contain the same three tokens, so "man" gets the same output in each. That is why order must be injected explicitly.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Your index holds tweets whose lengths all fall between 25 and 35 tokens, and nothing else. You move b from 0.75 to 0.3. What do you expect?
options: Large ranking changes, because tweets vary in length
All scores become zero
Scores become probabilities
Small changes, because lengths are all close to avgdl so B stays near 1 either way
explain: B = (1 - b) + b x |d|/avgdl. When every |d|/avgdl is near 1, B is near 1 for any b, so b has little effect. b matters most when lengths vary a lot.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: Someone computes $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2 + 1)$ at $x = 1$ and gets $1/2$. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; 1/2 is correct
They used 1/u with u = 2 but forgot to multiply by du/dx = 2x = 2; the answer is 1
They should have used 1/x, giving 1
The log has no derivative at 1
explain: Outer: $d\ln(u)/du = 1/u = 1/2$ at $u = 2$. Inner: $du/dx = 2x = 2$. The chain rule multiplies them: $1/2 \times 2 = 1$. Forgetting the inner factor is the most common chain-rule error.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: A script runs `for f in $(ls *.txt); do wc -l $f; done` in a folder containing `notes.txt` and `q3 report.txt`. What happens?
options: It works: the glob keeps each file name intact
wc is called on `notes.txt`, `q3` and `report.txt`, and fails on the last two
bash refuses to run because ls output cannot be expanded
Only `notes.txt` is processed because the loop stops at the first space
explain: The command substitution `$(ls *.txt)` is unquoted, so its output is word-split on whitespace, and `q3 report.txt` becomes two words. The fix is to let the glob produce the list directly: `for f in *.txt; do wc -l "$f"; done`. Globbing results are not split again.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: A batch contains the token IDs [2, 2, 4] and the model uses an embedding table with 5 rows. After one backward pass, which rows of the table have a nonzero gradient?
options: All 5 rows, because the whole matrix is a parameter
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient being the sum of two contributions
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient counted once because duplicates are removed
Only row 4, because repeated tokens cancel out
explain: Only looked-up rows get gradient, and a row looked up twice accumulates both contributions (the lookup's backward pass is a scatter-add). Rows 0, 1 and 3 get exactly zero, which is what makes sparse updates possible.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: contrastive learning and failure modes
question: You train a contrastive image model with $\tau = 1$ and unnormalized dot products. The contrastive loss falls nicely, but a linear classifier trained on the representation scores poorly. Which change does SimCLR's ablation most directly support?
options: Remove the negatives so the model only sees positives
Increase tau to 10 to smooth the loss
Take the representation from z instead of h
Use cosine similarity (l2 normalization) with a tuned, smaller temperature
explain: SimCLR reports that without l2 normalization the contrastive task gets easier but the representation is worse under linear evaluation, and that a proper temperature matters too. Removing negatives invites collapse (everything maps to one point), a larger tau flattens the softmax further, and h, not z, is the better representation.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
question: A server runs LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an 80 GB A100 with 2048-token contexts. Ignoring overheads, roughly how many full sequences fit in the KV space?
options: About 31
About 2,048
About 62
Unlimited, KV lives in host memory
explain: Each sequence needs 2048 x 512 KiB = 1 GiB (about 1.07 GB). 66.6 GB / 1.07 GB is about 62. Halving the context doubles how many fit.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: A colleague's loop `for j: for i: total += m[i][j]` over a large C 2D array of longs is slow. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Swap the loops so the inner loop walks j along a row
Use a faster add instruction
Make total a global variable
Add more threads before changing anything
explain: In C, m[i][j] and m[i][j+1] are adjacent, so walking j in the inner loop uses all 8 longs of every 64-byte line it fetches. The current inner loop strides a full row per access, fetching a new line every time.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: A model with a 50,000-token vocabulary predicts the uniform distribution at every position. What is its average cross-entropy loss?
options: 0 nats, because it never assigns zero probability
About 10.8 nats, which is ln(50,000)
About 0.69 nats, which is ln(2)
50,000 nats
explain: Uniform means p(target) = 1/50,000 everywhere, so the loss is -ln(1/50,000) = ln(50,000), about 10.82 nats. Real training starts near this value and falls as the model learns.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: In the toy, which beta gives the best true quality among the ones shown, and why is the smallest beta not best?
options: beta = 0.1, because it has the highest reward model score
beta = 1, because past it the policy shifts mass to the response the reward model overrates
beta = 100, because any change from SFT hurts
All are equal, because the reward model is unbiased on average
explain: True quality is 0.27 at beta = 1 versus 0.24 at 0.5 and -0.38 at 0.1. Small beta lets the policy concentrate on Flattery, which the reward model overrates. Some optimization helps: beta = 100 leaves quality at 0.10.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
question: Given `int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; **pp = 9;`, what is the value of x?
options: 5, because only pp was assigned
It is undefined behavior
The address of p
explain: *pp is the object pp points to, which is p. **pp follows p one more step, reaching x. Assigning 9 through it writes into x. All of this is well defined because every pointer points to a live object of the right type.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: A teammate says: 'Our test suite passes under AddressSanitizer, so the parser has no buffer overflows.' What is the right response?
options: Correct, ASan proves the absence of memory errors
ASan only checks stack memory, so heap overflows could remain
ASan only reports errors on paths the tests executed; untested inputs can still overflow
ASan cannot detect overflows, only leaks
explain: ASan checks accesses that actually happen at run time, on heap, stack and globals. It does not reason about inputs you never ran. Combine it with broad tests or fuzzing (running the code on huge numbers of generated inputs) to cover more paths.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Slices and why references cannot dangle
question: Why does returning `&s[0..5]` from `first_word` prevent the clear-then-use bug, when returning the index 5 did not?
options: Slices are copied, so clearing `s` does not affect them
The slice is a borrow of `s`, so any `&mut s` (like `clear`) while it is still used is a compile error
`clear` checks at run time whether slices exist
explain: The borrow checker tracks the slice as a shared borrow of `s`. `clear` needs a mutable borrow, and shared XOR mutable makes the overlap illegal. There is no run-time check involved.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: $A$ has shape $3 \times 5$. Which input can it multiply, and what comes out?
options: A vector with 5 components; out comes a vector with 3
A vector with 3 components; out comes a vector with 5
Any vector; out comes a 3 x 5 matrix
A vector with 15 components; out comes a scalar
explain: Each row has 5 entries and is dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so $\mathbf{x}$ needs 5 components. There are 3 rows, so 3 output components. An $m \times n$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
question: A loss is quadratic with curvature 40 along its sharpest direction. Which learning rate makes plain gradient descent diverge?
explain: Stability needs $\eta < 2/40 = 0.05$. At 0.06 the factor is $1 - 40(0.06) = -1.4$, so the error grows by 40 percent per step with alternating sign. 0.025 is the one-step optimum $1/40$; 0.045 oscillates but still converges (factor -0.8).

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: An MLP maps a 784-pixel image through one hidden layer of 100 units to 10 class scores. How many parameters (weights plus biases) does it have?
explain: Layer 1: 784 x 100 weights + 100 biases = 78,500. Layer 2: 100 x 10 weights + 10 biases = 1,010. Total 79,510. Forgetting biases gives 79,400.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Under a purely cooperative OS (no timer interrupt), a process enters `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. What happens?
options: The OS never runs again on that CPU; in practice the machine must be rebooted
The OS notices after one time slice and preempts it
The trap table automatically jumps to the scheduler after a while
The process is killed because infinite loops are privileged operations
explain: With no timer interrupt, the OS only regains control when the process makes a system call or does something illegal. An infinite loop does neither, so the OS cannot run. OSTEP notes the only recourse is to reboot. This is exactly why the timer interrupt exists.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: disks, inodes and crash-safe journaling
question: In data journaling, why must the file system wait for TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and Db to finish before writing TxE, instead of issuing all five writes at once?
options: Because the disk can only accept one write at a time
Because TxE must be written to the final location, not the journal
Because the disk may reorder a large write; TxE could land before Db, and replay would then copy garbage as if it were committed
Because waiting makes the journal smaller
explain: Disks schedule writes internally. If all five are issued together, TxE might hit the disk while Db has not. After a crash the transaction looks committed, and recovery would checkpoint garbage. Writing TxE only after the rest completes, as an atomic 512-byte write, closes the window.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
question: Which statement does the central limit theorem actually support?
options: With enough data, the individual data points become normally distributed
The sample mean of many i.i.d. finite-variance samples is approximately normal
Any average is normal, even of strongly correlated samples
Large samples remove bias from a skewed sampling method
explain: The CLT is about the distribution of the average (or sum), not the raw data: individual clicks are still 0 or 1. It needs independence and finite variance, and it says nothing about bias: a biased sample averages tightly around the wrong value.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
question: Using $C \approx 6ND$, roughly how much compute does a 405B-parameter model trained on 15.6T tokens use?
options: About 3.8e25 FLOPs
About 6.3e24 FLOPs
About 1.3e25 FLOPs
About 2.5e26 FLOPs
explain: $6 \times 4.05\times10^{11} \times 1.56\times10^{13} \approx 3.8e+25$ FLOPs, which matches the 3.8e25 Meta reports for Llama 3 405B. 6.3e24 forgets the factor 6; 1.3e25 uses 2N (inference cost) instead of 6N.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A legal team must find every contract mentioning a clause before a court deadline, and a junior reviewer will read whatever is returned. Which metric should you optimize first?
options: Precision at 1
Recall (at a generous cutoff)
Accuracy over the whole collection
Precision at 10
explain: Missing a relevant contract is the costly error, and the team will read through extra results, so recall matters most. P@1 and P@10 measure only the top of the list, and accuracy is dominated by the huge number of true negatives.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your service embeds documents in batches of 32. The same document gets clearly different vectors depending on which batch it lands in. What is the most likely bug?
options: The model is non-deterministic because of dropout at inference
Cosine similarity is unstable for vectors of length 1
Mean pooling is averaging over padding positions instead of using the attention mask
The tokenizer lowercases differently per batch
explain: Padding length depends on the longest text in the batch, so if pooling ignores the attention mask, the number and effect of [PAD] rows changes with batch composition. Dropout is disabled in eval mode, and tokenization does not depend on the batch.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
question: You double a model's vocabulary size, keeping everything else fixed. Which pair of effects should you expect?
options: Longer sequences and a smaller embedding table
No change in sequence length, only more parameters
Shorter token sequences for the same text, and a larger embedding table
Shorter sequences and fewer parameters
explain: More vocabulary entries let the tokenizer keep longer pieces, so the same text needs fewer tokens. But each new entry is another row of $d$ numbers in the embedding table (and in the output layer that predicts the next token).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: Your model is weak at multi-digit addition, and you are designing the tokenizer for its successor. Which change most directly targets the problem?
options: Double the vocabulary so more numbers become single tokens
Remove the end-of-text token
Make numbers tokenize consistently, for example one token per digit as LLaMA does
Switch from UTF-8 to UTF-16 bytes
explain: The problem is that the same digits land in different token groupings depending on what BPE happened to merge. Splitting digits individually (LLaMA) or into fixed-size groups (cl100k) gives a consistent structure. A bigger vocabulary makes more numbers single opaque tokens, which hides their digits from the model.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout: train mode vs eval mode
question: You train a model whose batches have only 2 examples per GPU and see unstable results. Which normalization is the natural fix?
options: BatchNorm with momentum 0.01
LayerNorm, since its statistics come from each example alone
Increase dropout to 0.9
Remove the learned gamma and beta
explain: Batch statistics from 2 examples are extremely noisy. LayerNorm's mean and variance are computed over one example's features, so batch size does not matter. The LayerNorm paper names batch-size dependence as the limitation it was designed to remove.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: Your HNSW service hits 99 percent recall@10 but p99 latency is too high. Memory is fine and you cannot rebuild today. What is the right first move?
options: Lower M
Lower ef and re-measure recall vs latency
Lower ef_construction
Switch the metric from cosine to L2
explain: ef is the only knob that applies without a rebuild; M and ef_construction are fixed at build time. Our sweep shows recall saturates near the top, so a modest drop in ef can cut work substantially for a small recall loss.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: Spot the bug in this load loop: `t0 = now(); send(req); resp = recv(); hist.record(now() - t0)` run back to back on 16 connections.
options: It records in milliseconds instead of microseconds
It measures from actual send time on closed-loop connections, so requests delayed while the connection was blocked are never counted
It should use the mean instead of a histogram
Nothing, 16 connections make it open-loop
explain: Each connection only sends after the previous reply, and t0 is taken at actual send. Time a request spent waiting to be sent during a stall is invisible. Fix: drive sends from a rate plan and record now() minus the intended send time.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: A developer writes `merged[-1][1] = e` instead of `max(merged[-1][1], e)`. On the toy resume (generous convention), what total does the code report?
options: 132 months, the bug never triggers
180 months, it stops merging
129 months: B, nested inside A, cuts A's block short by 3 months
137 months, gaps are counted
explain: When B (ending Dec 2017) is merged into A's block, the end is overwritten from Mar 2018 to Dec 2017, losing Jan to Mar 2018. C still starts a new block, D and E extend it correctly, so the total is 31 + 98 = 129. Nested intervals are exactly the case max() exists for.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: In the Titans update, the model sets alpha_t close to 1 at some token. What does that do?
options: Writes this token's value with maximum strength
Clears almost all of the memory before adding the current update
Freezes the memory so this token is ignored
Carries all of the previous surprise into this step
explain: alpha_t multiplies the old memory by (1 - alpha_t). Near 1 that wipes the memory, which is useful at a hard context boundary. Write strength is theta_t; carrying past surprise is eta_t.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
question: A CPU with loaded-plus-previous magazines (M = 10) runs a burst of 1,000 allocations with no frees, starting with a full loaded magazine and an empty previous one. About how many depot visits does it make?
options: About 1, the previous magazine absorbs the rest
About 100
About 500
About 1,000
explain: One-sided runs are exactly the case the 1/M bound describes. Each depot trip delivers one full magazine of 10 rounds, so 1,000 allocations need roughly 1,000 / 10 = 100 trips (the first 10 come from the magazine already loaded).

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
question: On the test year, seasonal naive has MAE 24.25 and naive has MAE 37.92. What would most directly remove seasonal naive's remaining error on this series?
options: Use a smaller alpha
Switch from MAE to RMSE
Use only the last 12 months of training data
Add a trend term, since all its errors are positive by roughly one year of growth
explain: Every seasonal naive error is positive, between 19 and 30, close to 12 months x 2 per month = 24. That is a systematic bias from ignoring the trend. A method with both trend and season terms (Holt-Winters, next lesson) addresses it. Changing the metric changes the score, not the forecast.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
question: Which version of the store line is a bug when N is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE?
options: tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=offsets < n_elements)
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y)
None of them; tl.store never writes out of bounds
explain: Without a mask the last program writes all BLOCK_SIZE lanes, including addresses past the end of the output buffer. That corrupts neighboring memory or faults. The first two are the same mask written two ways.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
question: A tokenizer downsamples by 16 in each direction. How many image positions does a 512 x 512 image take, not counting BOI and EOI?
explain: 512 / 16 = 32 per side, and 32 x 32 = 1024. This matches Chameleon, whose tokenizer turns a 512 x 512 image into 1024 tokens. 32 is only one side; 4096 is what an f = 8 tokenizer gives.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
question: In the Janus ablation, replacing the shared VQ tokenizer with decoupled SigLIP + VQ raised MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4 while FID moved from 8.72 to 8.53. What does that suggest?
options: Generation quality was the bottleneck
The transformer was too small
A reconstruction-oriented tokenizer gives poor semantic features for understanding, and a dedicated understanding encoder fixes that without hurting generation
MMBench rewards image resolution only
explain: Generation was about the same in both rows, so the gain is almost all understanding. VQ codes are trained to rebuild pixels, not to expose meaning; SigLIP is trained to align images with text.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
question: Mirage seals a unikernel so no page table changes are allowed after start of day. Which consequence must the application live with?
options: It cannot receive network packets
It must pre-allocate all the memory it needs at startup, since the heap cannot grow by mapping new pages
It cannot use a garbage collector
It must run with a single vCPU
explain: The paper states a sealed VM cannot expand its heap and must pre-allocate its memory at boot; allocation within the heap and I/O mappings still work. The single vCPU in Mirage is a separate design choice, not a consequence of sealing.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
question: hnswlib prefetches `vector_of(data[j + 1])`. For a 768-d fp32 vector, what does that one instruction bring toward the cache?
options: All 3,212 bytes of the next neighbor's block
One 64-byte cache line at the start of the next neighbor's vector
The whole neighbor list of the next neighbor
Nothing on ARM builds without SSE, and everything on x86
explain: A prefetch hint covers the cache line containing the address. Here that is the first line of the vector. The remaining lines rely on the hardware stream prefetcher once the distance loop starts reading.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
question: data.train_batch_size=512, rollout.n=8, actor.ppo_mini_batch_size=128, ppo_epochs=1. How many actor optimizer steps happen per RL step?
explain: 512 prompts x 8 = 4096 responses. The mini-batch is 128 prompts, which the trainer scales to 128 x 8 = 1024 responses. 4096 / 1024 = 4 optimizer steps. Reading ppo_mini_batch_size as responses would give 32, the common mistake.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem
question: You must answer questions about 2-second events in 30-minute videos and can afford 256 frames. Which statement is right?
options: Uniform sampling hits about 28% of such events, so dense or question-aware selection is needed
Uniform sampling hits every event because 256 frames is a lot
Random sampling would hit more events than a uniform grid
Hit rate does not depend on video length
explain: $P = \min(1, 2 \times 256 / 1800) \approx 0.284$. A grid always does at least as well as independent random times for the same N, and the hit rate falls as the video gets longer.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
question: A model scores 100% on a video needle-in-a-haystack test at 1 hour. What can you conclude?
options: It will answer any question about hour-long videos correctly
It can locate a single salient item anywhere in an hour of context; multi-event reasoning still needs benchmarks like Video-MME or LongVideoBench
Its frame sampling is uniform
It uses a memory bank
explain: A needle test isolates retrieval of one planted item. Real questions require combining several moments, ordering and counting, which is what the long splits of Video-MME and LongVideoBench's referring reasoning test.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
question: Generating 16 frames from one prompt frame with 25 MaskGIT steps per frame needs how many dynamics forward passes?
explain: The prompt frame is given, so 15 new frames are generated, each needing 25 passes: 15 x 25 = 375. This sequential cost is a big reason the original Genie ran near 1 FPS.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
question: Why does DeiT resize position embeddings with bicubic rather than bilinear interpolation?
options: Bicubic is faster on GPUs
Bilinear interpolation shrinks the vectors' norm, and short embeddings hurt the pretrained network
Bilinear cannot resize a 14x14 grid to 24x24 because 24 is not a multiple of 14
Bicubic interpolates the CLS embedding too, which bilinear cannot
explain: DeiT's stated reason is the norm: averaging neighbors shortens vectors, and those low-norm embeddings are out of distribution for the pretrained blocks. Both methods handle any target size, and the CLS embedding is not interpolated at all; it is kept as is.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens
question: A dimension has bounds [-0.05, 0.05] m and 256 uniform bins. For an action inside the bounds, what is the largest possible decoding error?
options: 0.39 mm, one full bin
0.195 mm, half a bin
0.05 m, half the range
Zero, because the token stores the exact value
explain: The bin width is 0.1 m / 256 = 0.39 mm. Decoding returns the bin center, so the worst case is a value at a bin edge: half a bin, 0.195 mm.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: A Diffusion Policy user raises the execution horizon from 8 to 64 steps on a task where objects get bumped. Success drops. Why?
options: Longer chunks are less smooth
The diffusion model cannot predict more than 16 steps
Longer execution horizons increase the number of denoising steps per action
The robot executes many actions without looking, so it reacts slowly when the scene changes
explain: Executing more steps open-loop improves consistency but delays the next observation. Diffusion Policy's ablation found too long a horizon hurts because of slow reaction time, with 8 steps best for most tasks.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images
question: Why did the VQGAN paper target 256 tokens per image rather than, say, 1024?
options: The codebook had only 256 entries
256 was the longest sequence they could feasibly train a 307M GPT-2 medium on with a 12 GB GPU
The perceptual loss only works on 16 x 16 grids
Longer sequences always give worse reconstructions
explain: The paper states 16 x 16 was the maximum feasible length for GPT-2 medium on a 12 GB GPU. The perceptual and adversarial losses were what made reconstructions at that strong compression good enough.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
question: On an A100 (SM 8.0) you start a BF16 model with `--attention-backend FLASHMLA`. The model is not MLA. What happens?
options: vLLM ignores the flag and uses FLASH_ATTN, the first valid entry
Startup fails with a ValueError listing reasons such as compute capability not supported and non-MLA not supported
FLASHMLA runs, but more slowly than FLASH_ATTN
vLLM switches to TRITON_MLA because it accepts any GPU
explain: An explicit backend is validated alone. FLASHMLA reports `is_mla()` as true and accepts only capability 9.x or 10.x, so `validate_configuration` returns reasons and `get_attn_backend_cls` raises. The design doc shows this same error format.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
question: Why does LLaVA feed the language model the patch grid rather than CLIP's single pooled image embedding?
options: The pooled embedding is not differentiable
The language model requires exactly 576 inputs
CLIP's pooled embedding is in the wrong numeric format
A single vector cannot hold fine details such as which number sits on which line, while a grid keeps local information
explain: A pooled vector summarizes the whole image, which works for retrieval. Reading and answering questions needs local detail, so LLaVA keeps one vector per patch. The token count is a design choice, not a requirement of the language model.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
question: Your receipt extractor scores well on DocVQA-style questions but often miscounts the number of line items on long receipts. What is the most effective fix?
options: Ask the model to count more carefully
Switch to detail low to reduce noise
Do not rely on the model's count: extract the item list and count it in code, and validate against the printed subtotal
Report the DocVQA score instead
explain: Counting is a documented weakness. Turning the count into an extraction task (list every item) and doing the arithmetic in code removes the weak step and gives you a checksum.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
question: In a fast-path-slow-path queue, the fast path is only lock-free. Why is each operation still wait-free?
options: Because the fast path is tried at most MAX_FAILURES times, and the slow path completes in a bounded number of steps thanks to helping
Because the fast path almost always succeeds in practice
Because fast and slow paths cannot run at the same time
Because MAX_FAILURES is set to the number of threads
explain: Wait-freedom is a worst-case property. The bound comes from capping the fast-path attempts and then relying on the wait-free slow path, whose bound comes from helping. It does not depend on the fast path usually succeeding, and the paper explicitly lets both paths run in parallel.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Inside the models: a multimesh GNN and a 3D Earth transformer
question: Pangu-Weather learns a different positional bias for windows at different latitudes. What assumption of a standard vision transformer does this remove?
options: That tokens must be square
That the same relative offset means the same thing everywhere in the image
That attention must be causal
That the number of channels is fixed
explain: Swin shares one relative-position bias across all windows, which suits translation-invariant images. On a lat-lon grid, one cell step spans a different distance and climate regime depending on latitude, so the bias is made position-specific.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Owner pops newest, thief steals oldest: why the ends matter
question: A worker's deque holds, from top to bottom, tasks of 40, 20, 10 and 5 units pushed by one recursive split. A thief steals once and the owner pops once. Which tasks do they get?
options: Thief 5, owner 40
Thief 40, owner 5
Thief 40, owner 20
Both race for 5
explain: Thieves take from the top, where the oldest and here largest task (40) sits. The owner pops the bottom, the newest (5). They only contend when exactly one task is left.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: Which change to the giving-up path reintroduces lost wakeups?
options: Removing the barrier between decrementing the searcher count and rechecking the queues
Starting the search at a random victim
Stealing half instead of one task
Capping searchers at half the workers
explain: The barrier makes the searcher's decrement visible before it rereads the queues, so a concurrent submitter either sees zero searchers (and wakes someone) or its task is seen by the recheck. The other choices affect efficiency, not correctness.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
question: Your team knows the exact token budget for a one-off production run and will never extend it. Which statement best matches the evidence?
options: With a known budget, a well-tuned decay over the whole run (for example linear to zero) can match or slightly beat WSD; WSD's main advantage is flexibility
WSD is strictly required, because cosine cannot reach the same loss
WSD is always at least 10% better in loss
Any schedule is fine as long as there is warmup
explain: Hägele et al. found cooldowns roughly match tuned cosine, and Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero about 0.84% better than WSD at 80 tokens per parameter. WSD shines when the end date is uncertain or many lengths are needed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
question: An engineer benchmarks MSG_ZEROCOPY between two processes on one machine over 127.0.0.1 and sees no gain. Most likely reason?
options: MSG_ZEROCOPY only works for UDP
The SO_ZEROCOPY option resets on loopback
Packets looped to a local socket always incur a deferred copy
Loopback has no error queue
explain: The kernel converts zero-copy packets to private copies on paths that loop back to local sockets, to bound how long pages stay pinned. The docs warn that such a test will not show any improvement; benchmark between two hosts.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
question: A team measured p_cf with a zero-shot prompt, then switched to an 8-shot prompt with more technology examples and kept the old p_cf. What is the bug?
options: None; p_cf depends only on the model weights
p_cf should have been measured on the test set
Calibration only applies to zero-shot prompts
The bias is contextual: new examples change majority and recency bias, so p_cf must be re-measured with the new prompt
explain: Zhao et al. stress that the error is contextual: a different choice, order, or format of examples changes the content-free prediction. Adding technology examples would likely push the model further toward technology, which the stale p_cf does not account for.
